title: He Survived BOTH Atomic Bombs in 3 Days
description: Discover the incredible true story of Tsutomu Yamaguchi, the man who survived both the Hiroshima and Nagasaki atomic blasts just 72 hours apart. How would you react if history repeated itself like this?
script:
It sounds like a statistical impossibility that defies the laws of probability: surviving a nuclear blast at ground zero, only to travel directly to the hypocenter of a second atomic bomb three days later—and surviving both.

On the morning of August 6, 1945, Tsutomu Yamaguchi, a 29-year-old naval engineer for Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, was completing a three-month business trip in Hiroshima. At 8:15 AM, as he walked toward the shipyards, the United States bomber Enola Gay dropped 'Little Boy,' the world's first deployed atomic weapon. The bomb exploded 1,900 feet above the city, unleashing a thermal flash reaching millions of degrees Celsius and a shockwave traveling faster than the speed of sound. Yamaguchi was located just three kilometers from ground zero. The instantaneous burst ruptured his eardrums, temporarily blinded him, and left severe radiation burns across the left side of his upper body.

Despite his agonizing injuries, Yamaguchi spent a fitful night in an air-raid shelter before making his way through the ash and charred ruins to Hiroshima’s train station. Miraculously, despite massive destruction, evacuation trains were still operating. He boarded an overnight train filled with refugees, traveling nearly 200 miles southwest back to his hometown: Nagasaki.

Arriving home on August 8, Yamaguchi received basic medical treatment and insisted on reporting to Mitsubishi's Nagasaki office the following morning, August 9. Bandaged, pale, and suffering from acute radiation exposure, he tried explaining the terrifying weapon to his disbelieving executive supervisor. His boss openly scoffed at the report, insisting that a single bomb could not possibly vaporize a modern metropolis.

At precisely 11:02 AM, mid-sentence as his manager questioned his sanity, the sky above Nagasaki tore open. The 'Fat Man' plutonium bomb detonated three kilometers overhead. The shockwave blew out the reinforced office windows, tearing off Yamaguchi’s fresh bandages and throwing him to the ground. Yet again, structural shielding and incredible fortune saved his life.

Yamaguchi became one of the few humans to endure two nuclear attacks at close range. Recognized officially by the Japanese government as a nijū hibakusha—a double atomic bomb survivor—Yamaguchi lived to the age of 93, dedicating his final years to advocating for global nuclear disarmament.
